title: Berkshire Hathaway: Are Warren Buffett & Co. Losing Their Midas Touch? - Berkshire Hathaway A (NYSE:BRK.A)
text:
Introduction Last week, we had an interesting discussion on our chat room regarding the high level of cash, about $103.64B (or 34.6% of the liquid-invested portfolio), that Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A )( BRK.B ) maintain on its balance sheet.
It started with a question by one of our subscribers (12/4/2018, after the close):
On a red day like this, everyone moans and groans. But I was reminded about a key comment from a friend earlier today that I think is paramount. We all track Warren Buffett's latest stock moves, but we forget his largest position. Take a guess? No it's not Apple or the banks. 103 Billion in cash and 202 Billion in equities, that's 33%.. I suspect Seth Klarman and Prem Wasta are in similar positions. I'm curious about your thoughts? @trapping.value @the.fortune.teller For me I have kept 20% in cash, and my rule to drop that to zero would be a 2008 drop.
This article is a detailed version of the discussion we held about this subject/question.

$299,527,418,682 100.00% BRK's Portfolio as at 9/30/2018 - Main Changes Berkshire Hathaway's latest 13-F reveals that Warren Buffett's holding company added few interesting positions during the third quarter of 2018:
Over 35.6M shares in JPMorgan ( JPM ) Over 41.4M shares in Oracle ( ORCL ) Over 6M shares in PNC Financial ( PNC ) Over 3.5M shares in Travelers ( TRV ) Contrary to these new positions, the company got out of its positions in Walmart ( WMT ) and Sanofi ( SNY ).
Here's how these changes have performed during the fourth quarter QTD:
WMT Total Return Price data by YCharts
BRK itself (using the midpoint of -4.08% between BRK.A to BRK.B) has outperformed the main indices by a wide margin - ~3.24% against the DIA, ~5.26% against the SPY, and ~9% (!!!) against the QQQ.
Nonetheless, those are neither the additions and certainly not the positions BRK exited from during the third quarter that allowed BRK to outperform.
The two positions BRK exited from (WMT and SNY) have actually outperformed everything else (in this comparison): i) BRK itself, ii) the main indices (SPY, DIA and QQQ) and iii) the new additions (JPM, ORCL, PMC, and TRV)
All four additions have under-performed BRK, with TRV being the closest one, but PNC, JPM and mainly ORCL performing far worse than the holding company. Having said that, ORCL has performed muck better than the QQQ or the technology sector ( XLK ).
Let's not forget that Warren Buffett and Jamie Dimon (JPM's CEO) have great respect to each other. Buffett already "admitted" that he reads Dimon's (the longest-tenured of CEOs leading a major US bank) annual shareholder letter in order to gain insights into the banking industry.
In January, the two - together with Jeff Bezos, Amazon's ( AMZN ) CEO - announced that they are forming a partnership aiming at cutting healthcare ( XLV ) costs and improving the services their employees in the US get.
BRK's Largest Positions as at 9/30/2018 - Performance Here's how BRK's largest positions have performed during the fourth quarter of this year, thus far:
KO Total Return Price data by YCharts
If we are to make a sample-smaller portfolio only out of these largest positions, the total return QTD would be as follows:
Source: Author
The good news is that BRK still manages to outperform the SPY.
The bad news is that BRK's two largest positions are the first and third worst-performers among these 12-position portfolio. In more simple words, the company is holdings very large positions in companies that are performing much worse than the markets as well as BRK's other positions.
This leads us to the next topic, which is the most troubling of them all.
Very High Concentration on Very Few Sectors Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio as at 9/30/2018 shows that the "Oracle of Omaha" is now very much concentrated on three sectors:
1. Financials ( XLF ): 42.57% of IP vs. 16.18% weighting in the SPY.
Berkshire truly believes in the US banking system. The company's second- and third-largest positions behind AAPL, are BAC and WFC. So much so that during Q3, stake in BAC increased by 29%. Per their 13-F filing, Berkshire also added to its already large stakes in USB, GS and BK.
Thing is that this is coming at a very suspicious-troubled time for banks.
On one hand, there are macro issues, such as the China-US trade war/tariffs , the changes European fiscal and monetary policies , and most of all - the risk of a recession .
On the other hand, you have banking specific issues, such as the looming threat an inverted yield curve , as well as the "too big to fall" issue that is surely contagious.
Shrinking spreads means lower profitability. That's on top of the trading activity which isn't great, to say the least, based on what top executives of two major US banks - JPM's CEO Jamie Dimon and Citigroup's ( C ) CFO John Gerspach - said last week.
2. Technology ( XLK ): 24.68% of IP vs. 21.68% weighting in the SPY.
It's not the 3% higher allocation that catches the eye here, rather the 21.72% allocation to a single stock - Apple. Even if we account for the cash portion, APPL weighting remains a whooping 14.2%.
Even if one choose to ignore the issues related to the technology sector , it's hard - and unwarranted to ignore the specific issues surrounding Apple .
Taiwan's Largan Precision ( OTC:LGANF ) is the most recent supplier of AAPL to report significant decline in revenue and/or orders, mostly/entirely associated with the second-, on the verge on becoming only the third-, largest stock from a market cap perspective.
MSFT Market Cap data by YCharts
Neither Microsoft ( MSFT ) recapturing the top spot nor Amazon ( AMZN ) trading less than $3B behind AAPL is what catching the eye in the above chart. What's alarming is how quickly (slightly over two months) AAPL - the stock ever belonging to the >$1T club - has lost over $300B of its market-cap.
Sure thing, BRK has started its investment in AAPL low enough to still sit on a significant gain. However, the fact that BRK keeps buying into the rotting (?) Apple is raising doubts and possibly may shift the gain into a loss should Apple shares won't reverse their downtrend soon.
Overshadowed by the new $4B stake in JPM, BRK also increased its AAPL holding by about 522,802 shares, during Q3/2018. With this additional investment, Berkshire Hathaway owns (as of 9/30/2018) a bit over 5% of all Apple's outstanding shares.
I must admit that this is the first time that I see Warren Buffett adhering to one of his famous statements:
Diversification is protection against ignorance. It makes little sense if you know what you are doing.
3. Consumer Staples ( XLP ): 18.65% of IP vs. 7.79% weighting in the SPY (also known as " Consumer Defensive") .
At least on that part, I can't say we disagree, as evident by our recent pieces:

Bottom Line The title of this article is asking whether Warren Buffett & Co. might be losing their Midas Touch ?
If one is looking at the total return of Berkshire Hathaway since its initial public offering date of May 9th, 1996 - the answer is NO.
Nonetheless, if we are examining the performance of the Oracle since March 9th, 2009, when the subprime crisis ended - the answer is not that clear.
Start investing in AAPL back in 1996 or even 2009 would have served BRK much better than doing so in 2017; certainly in 2018.
Just as I wouldn't go that far calling AAPL a rotten/poisonous Apple, I wouldn't dare declaring that the Oracle of Omaha has lost its Midas Touch. What he may have forgotten - we will never learn!
Having said that, when it comes to the level of cash Berkshire Hathaway is keeping on its balance sheet - I must repeat what I've wrote to the Wheel of FORTUNE 's subscribers:
BRK made a killing here, but my point (responding to the question about them holding 1/3 in cash) was that they hold that much of cash because when you have such a high concentrations in few (quite volatile) stocks/sectors - the cushion musts be bigger.
I'm not implying that Buffett/BRK did bad with holding $AAPL - we all know they did very well - but truth must be told: 24% in one stock (out of the invested part; 15% from the total) is NOT something to be praised. Same goes with the exposure to financials at a time when spreads are contracting.
Of course, the liquid portfolio is only part of BRK's overall investments so you can say that if we count for all assets - those are reasonable exposures. Yet, since I've been asked about the cash element of the liquid portfolio - I found it important to note that this isn't a portfolio I suggest anyone to copy.
Btw, this morning starts on the wrong foot for AAPL as another supplier reports major decline in revenues/orders.
I'm not against cash; quite the contrary. However, unlike many investors, cash for me is dry powder, i.e. free margin. Once again to quote one of my posts:
For me the "cash" element = free margin. I always leave room for the next best thing. If one operates with no margin (cash only) then sure - some needs to be in cash. Let's not also forget that BRK's $202B portfolio has 24% in one stock ( AAPL ) that hasn't performed so well lately. Then 12% & 11% in BAC and WFC, respectively, followed by 9% in KO, 8% in AXP and KHC ,each, 3.5% in USB, 2% in JPM, BK, MCO, DAL and GS (each).
